articles.title: Two Chinese win world's top Maths prize for solving century-old problems
articles.summary: This is the first time Chinese nationals have won the prestigious Fields Medal.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Mathematicians Yu Deng and Hong Wang are China's first Fields Medal recipients By Joel Guinto   and   Fan Wang 
- Published 24 July 2026 
Two Chinese academics have won the world's top prize for mathematics for the first time, according to state media. 
Chinese mathematicians Hong Wang and Yu Deng won alongside John Pardon from the US and Jacon Tsimerman from Canada. They each won 15,000 Canadian dollars ($10,500; £8,000). 
Both won for solving problems that have baffled mathematicians for more than a century. And 35-year-old Wang, who teaches in the US and France, is only the third woman to receive the honour. 
The Fields Medal, regarded as the Nobel prize equivalent for mathematics, was handed out on Thursday in the US as human computations are increasingly challenged by AI. 
The achievement has made waves on Chinese social media. 
The hashtags "Fields Medal" and "First Chinese mathematicians to win Fields Medals" generated millions of views across various social media platforms from Weibo to Rednote. 
"Pride of all Chinese people," a comment from a Weibo user reads. 
"We are witnessing history," another said. 
Chinese media also extensively covered the two academics, with articles detailing everything from their educational backgrounds and personal interests to what their achievement means for the country. 
"For the Chinese mathematics community, this is a dream we have been hoping to realise for decades," said Shing-Tung Yau, the first ethnic Chinese Fields medallist. 
Together with her colleague, Josh Zahl, Wang answered a question posed by Japanese mathematician Soichi Kakeya in 1917: If you rotate a pencil so as to turn it completely around, what is the smallest area it sweeps out? 
Wang and Zahl analysed the problem on the assumption that the pencil was floating in a three-dimensional space, rather than on a flat surface. They published their study last year. 
"If this conjecture fascinates people so much, it is because this kind of phenomenon shows up naturally in problems from very different fields," Wang told AFP News Agency. 
Deng, a 37-year-old mathematics professor at the University of Chicago, was honoured for his work solving another century-old problem. 
In 1900, German mathematician David Hilbert asked what would become known as Hilbert's Sixth Problem: how the behaviour of a whole can be calculated based on the movement of individual particles. 
Deng solved the problem by looking at the behaviour of gases. 
He said it is a "really great honour to have my name listed after all those great mathematicians I've always been admiring". 
Wang has worked in harmonic analysis, which looks into the movement of waves. 
The Fields Medal is given every four years to outstanding mathematicians under the age of 40. 
Born in China, trained abroad 
Born in 1991 in the tourist city of Guilin in the southern region of Guangxi, Wang skipped two grades in primary school and was admitted to China's prestigious Peking University in 2007 at the age of 16. 
Although she initially majored in earth sciences, she transferred to the mathematics department a year later. 
After graduating, she pursued further studies abroad, studying at Paris-Sud University and the École Polytechnique in France, and earned her doctorate at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT). 
She is now a professor at New York University and a permanent professor at France's Institut des Hautes Études Scientifiques (IHES). 
On Thursday night, she received a phone call from French President Emmanuel Macron, who congratulated her on receiving the medal. "She embodies the excellence of our research and our training," Macron said in a post on X. "Choose France for science," he added. 
Deng, who began taking part in mathematics competitions while in primary school, was admitted to Peking University in 2007 - the same year as Wang - but transferred to MIT in 2009. 
He earned his doctorate from Princeton University and has been teaching at the University of Chicago since 2024.

articles.summary: Noul is the strongest typhoon to make landfall in China so far this year, state media reportedTyphoon Noul made landfall early Sunday bringing winds and heavy rain to southern China, including Hong Kong, over the weekend.It prompted the evacuation of hundreds of thousands of people in Guangdong province with the region on high alert and hundreds of flights cancelled. Typhoon Noul has caused widespread damage in southern China, including in Hong Kong. Photograph: Venron Yuen/Nexpher/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock 
View image in fullscreen 
Typhoon Noul has caused widespread damage in southern China, including in Hong Kong. Photograph: Venron Yuen/Nexpher/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock 
Typhoon Noul forces more than 715,000 from homes and cancels hundreds of flights in China and Hong Kong
Noul is the strongest typhoon to make landfall in China so far this year, state media reported 
Typhoon Noul made landfall early Sunday bringing winds and heavy rain to southern China, including Hong Kong , over the weekend. 
It prompted the evacuation of hundreds of thousands of people in Guangdong province with the region on high alert and hundreds of flights cancelled. 
China’s national weather centre said Noul made landfall along the Huidong county coast in the city of Huizhou in southern Guangdong province at approximately 3:50 am Sunday. China’s official Xinhua news agency said Noul was the strongest typhoon to make landfall in China so far this year. Weather tracker: More than 900 wildfires rage across Canada 
Read more 
Hong Kong’s Observatory said Noul, with maximum sustained winds of 110 km/h (68 mph) near its centre, was moving Sunday into inland Guangdong and weakening progressively, bringing strong winds and heavy rain to parts of the region. 
More than 715,000 people had been relocated for safety in Guangdong province, according to state-owned China National Radio. Train services in the province were cancelled for Sunday, according to the China News Service. 
China’s National Meteorological Center expected parts of southern Guangdong and south-eastern Fujian provinces to experience heavy rain and strong winds over the weekend. Many trees were seen uprooted in Huilai county, located on the coast of Guangdong province, state broadcaster CCTV reported. 
View image in fullscreen 
People brave the heavy wind and rain as they cross a street in Hong Kong. Photograph: Tyrone Siu/Reuters 
Hong Kong’s airport authority said about 350 flights were cancelled Sunday. At least nine people were injured across the city during the typhoon period, according to Hong Kong authorities. 
As Noul approached Hong Kong, parts of a large scaffolding on a high-rise building collapsed Saturday afternoon, local police said, although initial reports indicated there were no injuries. 
Taiwan’s Central Weather Administration said Noul was bringing rainfall to parts of southern and eastern Taiwan. It was passing over waters south of Taiwan, and was moving away from the island on Saturday. 
Earlier this month, Typhoon Bavi brought strong winds and rain to eastern China, leading to the evacuation of more than 2 million people. It made landfall on 11 July. Another, Maysak, made landfall in southern China on 3 July.

articles.title: How Chinese tech and Russian tactics are aiding Iran’s bombing of US bases
articles.summary: Increasingly accurate and lethal attacks are revealing weaknesses in stretched defences across the GulfAs the crisis in the Middle East escalates, Iran has been bombing US bases and critical infrastructure in the Gulf with increasing accuracy, helped by Chinese satellite imagery and tactics learned by Russia in Ukraine.Three US soldiers were killed last Friday in an attack on the Muwaffaq Salti airbase in Jordan, which was being protected by a Thaad air defence system. Satellite imagery later released by Iranian media showed several buildings had been destroyed. Continue reading...
articles.full_text:
An Iranian couple rides a motorbike past Iranian missiles, Zolfaghar, on display at Azadi Square in Tehran. Photograph: Abedin Taherkenareh/EPA 
View image in fullscreen 
An Iranian couple rides a motorbike past Iranian missiles, Zolfaghar, on display at Azadi Square in Tehran. Photograph: Abedin Taherkenareh/EPA Analysis 
How Chinese tech and Russian tactics are aiding Iran’s bombing of US bases
Dan Sabbagh Defence and security editor 
Increasingly accurate and lethal attacks are revealing weaknesses in stretched defences across the Gulf 
As the crisis in the Middle East escalates, Iran has been bombing US bases and critical infrastructure in the Gulf with increasing accuracy, helped by Chinese satellite imagery and tactics learned by Russia in Ukraine. 
Three US soldiers were killed last Friday in an attack on the Muwaffaq Salti airbase in Jordan, which was being protected by a Thaad air defence system. Satellite imagery later released by Iranian media showed several buildings had been destroyed. 
It is not clear why the air defence system failed in that incident, which is under Pentagon investigation, but it is a reminder that Iran retains an effective missile capability that its new leadership is willing to deploy . Almost 100 troops injured in recent weeks, Pentagon admits, as Iran launches reprisals on US allies 
Read more 
Andreas Krieg, an associate professor at the school of security studies, King’s College London, said a combination of better intelligence, missile navigation, manoeuvrability and coordinated attack planning amounted to “a real transformation”. 
It was the product, Krieg said, of three years of technological development of Iran’s ballistic missile programme, which remained roughly 70% intact on US intelligence estimates , despite previous claims from Washington that Tehran’s military capabilities had been obliterated. 
The first step was to use Chinese satellite imagery to help identify targets at US bases and other sites in the Gulf. The US imposed sanctions on three Chinese companies in May for providing such images. 
One, Mizar Vision, exposed the presence of US military aircraft and Patriot and Thaad air defence systems at bases in Saudi Arabia, Bahrain and the Jordanian base hit last week, and imagery released on social media was widely picked up. 
Some experts, however, said they were less sure Beijing had been providing intelligence. Sidharth Kaushal of the Royal United Services Institute said Iran had focused on static targets at US bases, for which commercial imagery was enough. 
“I haven’t seen anything where Iran has struck a target so dynamic that I’ve looked at this and gone ‘this has got to be foreign aid,’” he said. At the same time, however, questions have been raised about whether US bases, built to withstand attacks from insurgents, are sufficiently hardened against Iranian missile and drone attacks. 
A string of accurate Iranian attacks on CIA facilities across the Gulf during the bombings made US analysts wonder whether Russia had shared locations with Tehran, but the hypothesis is tentative. Has Trump dragged the US into a forever war in Iran? | Mohamad Bazzi 
Read more 
The US defence secretary, Pete Hegseth, told Congress this week that China and Russia were helping Iran to some extent. But Donald Trump contradicted him on Friday, saying Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin had personally assured him that they would not sell weapons to Iran. 
Iran’s ballistic programme relies heavily on Chinese electronics and ammonium perchlorate for rocket fuel, but the finished weapons are considered sophisticated enough to be able to occasionally defeat stretched US and Gulf air defences. 
Iranian missiles boast complex navigation, using GPS, China’s BeiDou and Russia’s Glonass simultaneously as they launch towards targets, and re-entry speeds, which are several times the speed of sound, always make anti-ballistic defence a challenge. 
Tehran has also developed “steerable warheads that can adjust their course during descent” on some of its ballistic missiles, Kreig said. Heat-seeking and optical navigation for the terminal phase means they are not vulnerable to electronic jamming because they are not using radio communication. 
All this is enough to present a serious challenge for US air defences at a time when stockpiles of Patriot and Thaad interceptors have been run down by about half after the 38-day US-Israel bombing campaign in the spring. Add in energy sites, oil refineries and desalination plants and there is a large area to cover. 
Iran has also evolved tactically in its missile attacks, using methods similar to Russia in Ukraine, where smaller salvoes can be more effective than larger ones, and drones are used to distract air defences, making way for a ballistic attack. 
Kaushal said he believed it was a case of the two countries’ militaries learning from each other’s experience – “a convergent evolution” – rather than it necessarily being the result of Moscow directly teaching Tehran. 
Though there is a degree of anti-western understanding between Iran, Russia and China, as well as North Korea, the so called “ axis of upheaval ” is far from a consistent military alliance. 
“There is a kind of collaboration there, but it doesn’t produce the kind of massive net benefits that Nato produces,” said Matthew Savill, a defence analyst from the Royal United Services Institute.

Mass job cuts loom at VW as profits fall steeply on China sales slump
Carmaker expects to sell 3% fewer vehicles this year as it pushes through a programme that could eliminate 100,000 roles 
Volkswagen has reported a steep fall in profits and cut its revenue forecast amid a sales slump in China , as the German carmaker pushes through a brutal cost-cutting programme that includes axeing up to 100,000 jobs. 
VW said it expects sales revenue to fall by up to 3% this year, a reversal of a previous forecast for a 3% increase on last year’s €321.9bn (£275.3bn), because of a sales slump in the highly competitive Chinese market. 
The sales slump will increase pressure on the world’s second-largest maker of vehicles to cut costs. Earlier this month VW’s supervisory board rejected the plans by the chief executive, Oliver Blume , to shut four factories in Germany, as the manufacturer confirmed it was raising the job cuts target to 100,000 , double the number already agreed by unions. Tesla stock suffers double-digit drop on carmaker’s worst day in years 
Read more 
Volkswagen’s operating profit fell by 9.5% to €3.5bn in the second quarter, below analysts’ estimates of a small increase to €3.9bn, as Blume battles with unions to push through a restructuring programme. 
On Friday the company said the proposed additional job cuts would mostly be in administrative positions across its global business. 
The plans also include reducing Volkswagen’s model line by up to half. 
Volkswagen employs more than 650,000 people across all its brands, which include Audi, Bentley, Skoda, Seat, Porsche and Cupra, and has been hit hard by growing – and cheap – Chinese competition and the struggle to shift to electric cars. 
In the first half of this year, Volkswagen delivered 6.3% fewer cars globally, about 4.1m, mostly because of its travails in China. 
Volkswagen sales in China have fallen by more than 31% in the first half, against increases in Europe and North America. 
“The extent to which western carmakers are being squeezed out of the Chinese car market by domestic operators is laid bare by Volkswagen’s latest update,” said Russ Mould, the investment director at AJ Bell. skip past newsletter promotion 
after newsletter promotion 
Blume said on Friday that Chinese carmakers had sharply increased exports, which was adding pressure in Europe. The restructuring was essential to make the company “more innovative, faster, more attractive and robust”. 
Volkswagen’s share price fell 1.5% after the release of its latest financial results and is down 66% over the past five years. 
“After nearly four years at the wheel as chief executive, Oliver Blume is likely to come under increasing pressure,” Mould said. “His plan to steer Volkswagen back on to a growth path involves drastically cutting costs, including by slashing the company’s headcount. There are also plans to reduce the number of models and sell off non-core assets to make Volkswagen a more efficient machine. Pushing these through may be difficult given likely opposition from unions, and whether they are enough to win over the market is an open question.” 
The tough market in China has also hit other carmakers, with BMW last month cutting its profit guidance for this year because of the disruption caused by the Iran war and the company’s struggles in the Chinese market.

Wildfire devastation in Ontario. Photograph: Chris Young/The Canadian Press/AP Analysis 
Weather tracker: More than 900 wildfires rage across Canada
James Michelin for MetDesk 
Fires remain out of control in Northwest Territories and Ontario, while Argentina endures record night-time heat 
Recent hot, dry weather in Canada has triggered hundreds of wildfires across the country. As of Wednesday, more than 900 were burning, scorching about 3m hectares of land. While fires have broken out in several provinces, the greatest concern is in the Northwest Territories and Ontario , where several remain out of control. 
Poor air quality has been reported across affected regions, with wildfire smoke carried by winds into the US and even across the Atlantic to northern Europe. The risk of further blazes remains high as North America enters the peak of fire season. 
Meanwhile, the city of Salta in Argentina recorded its warmest-ever overnight minimum temperature on Saturday, with the mercury failing to fall below 26C (79F). This reading is particularly remarkable because Argentina is in the middle of winter, when Salta’s average night-time minimum is about 3C. 
The previous warmest night at this weather station was 22.2C, recorded in January 1953 during the height of summer. This exceptional warmth was driven by the Zonda wind, which develops when westerly airflow crosses the Andes before descending, warming and drying as it sinks back to ground level. 
This process is known as the Foehn effect, a phenomenon that occurs on the downwind side of mountain ranges around the world. However, the intensity experienced in Salta last weekend was unusual. One contributing factor may have been the rapidly developing El Niño in the eastern Pacific, which would have left the incoming air mass warmer than average, even before it descended on the city. 
Elsewhere, the strengthening El Niño is also expected to increase typhoon activity in the western Pacific. Tropical Depression 11 formed on Tuesday before developing into Tropical Storm Noul north of the Philippines on Thursday night. The system is forecast to intensify into a typhoon over the coming days as it tracks between the Philippines and Taiwan, before making landfall on China’s south-east coast on Sunday morning local time as a category 1 storm.
